clue.text: Fancy keeping tailless cat, which is natural

indicators.note: without a tail, the word loses its final letter
to keep something is to hold it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: to fancy something is to like it
Felix the Cat, the cartoon character, minus his last letter

explanation.surface: Someone who likes cats with no tails finds the trait perfectly natural.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat is the cartoon character Felix, who loses his tail letter X before going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lifelike looks true to nature and real life, so natural is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Partners with newspaper in cloud

blocks.note: West and East are partners at the bridge table
FT is the Financial Times

explanation.surface: Two people share a newspaper while lost in a cloud of thought.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are North, South, East and West, and East and West play as partners. The FT is the Financial Times, a London newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists weft as a rare literary word for a thin film or wisp, such as a haze of smoke.

clue.text: Fool to mock inspiring holy man

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece takes the other inside it

blocks.note: to mock is to jeer
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: Someone is tempted to ridicule a saintly figure who motivates others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' reads as motivating, but here it means breathing in, taking the saint inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A jester was the professional fool kept at a royal court to amuse the king.

clue.text: On each side of street during a trip

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a trip is a ride

explanation.surface: Directions for passing along both pavements of a road on an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase; a preposition, so the answer must be one too.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit astride a horse is to have one leg on either flank, straddling it.

clue.text: Inclination in favour of Birmingham, perhaps, giving most of undead accommodation

indicators.note: most but not all means the final letter is dropped
to accommodate is to house a guest, so one piece is lodged inside

blocks.note: pro means for, in favour of
Birmingham is an example of a British city
not dead is live, shortened by a letter

explanation.surface: A liking for Birmingham suggests it has housing for zombies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undead' evokes vampires and zombies, but it simply means alive. Birmingham is England's second city.
explanation.definitionFit: A proclivity is a natural tendency or leaning towards something, just as an inclination is.

clue.text: Fine mistake: alien hunt

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
to err is to make a mistake
E.T., the film's extra-terrestrial

explanation.surface: Chasing extraterrestrials turns out to be a fine error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistake' gives the verb ERR rather than a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To ferret, or ferret about, is to search eagerly, as the animal does when flushing rabbits.

clue.text: Radio West broadcast series about trial's ending

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another
seed broadcast is scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for west
taken as written
the final letter of trial

explanation.surface: A western radio station airs a drama series following a court case to its conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radio' and 'broadcast' sit together naturally, hiding that the second word is a signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Wireless is the old-fashioned British name for a radio set, from transmitting without connecting cables.

clue.text: Cut up vehicle before its tax

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
VED is Vehicle Excise Duty, the British road tax on a car

explanation.surface: Someone who loses their car before paying its tax is cut up about it.
explanation.walkthrough: VED, Vehicle Excise Duty, is the annual tax on a road vehicle in Britain. 'Cut up' looks like upset, but it is slicing.
explanation.definitionFit: To carve meat is to slice it, so carved means cut up into portions.

clue.text: Purify can, else made ill

indicators.note: something made ill is out of sorts, so these letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to sterilise a tin, since otherwise someone gets sick.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits definition from fodder; 'made ill' reads as food poisoning but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleanse is to make thoroughly clean, removing dirt or impurity, so it matches purify.

clue.text: Subject of sermon is dry, tackling letter 24

indicators.note: a tackler wraps arms round the opponent, so one piece is held inside

blocks.note: TT, teetotal, means not drinking alcohol
the 24th letter of the alphabet is X, whose name is spelt EX

explanation.surface: A preacher's subject is dull as he works through a numbered letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter 24' looks like a cross-reference to 24-across, but it is the 24th letter of the alphabet, X, written as its name. TT means teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: A preacher's text is the Bible passage on which a sermon is based and expounded.

clue.text: Possible scenario for 2-1 match in '60

blocks.note: read as two words: in a game ending 2-1, three goals are scored in all
a score is twenty, so three of them make sixty

explanation.surface: Commentary on how a two-goals-to-one football game might have gone back in 1960.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes 60 look like the year 1960, but it is simply the number. The first half splits the answer into THREE SCORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so threescore is the old way of saying sixty, as in threescore years and ten.

clue.text: Reportedly, one beating strong drink

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: to lick someone is to beat them, so a licker is one beating

explanation.surface: Gossip says someone who gets violent has been drinking hard.
explanation.walkthrough: To lick is informal for to thrash or defeat, so the one doing it is a licker.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquor is alcoholic drink, especially distilled spirits such as whisky or gin.

clue.text: Playing tune in that place, daughter is lacking restraint

indicators.note: a musician playing freely improvises and varies the order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
there means in that place
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A daughter playing music over there is letting rip without inhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing tune' reads as one musical act, but the first word signals rearranging the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untethered is no longer tied or held back, so it is free of any restraint.

clue.text: Student is testing bottles one used to cure toothache

indicators.note: a bottle holds its contents inside, so the letters are held within the phrase

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles the three words

explanation.surface: A student researcher tries out bottled remedies for a sore tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like containers of medicine but is a verb meaning holds; the definition is the clue's tail end.
explanation.definitionFit: A dentist is the medical professional people visit to treat tooth decay and relieve aching teeth.

clue.text: Follower reacts badly before unknown

indicators.note: done badly means done wrong, so the letters come out in a muddled order

blocks.note: taken as written
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns

explanation.surface: A disciple responds poorly when faced with the unfamiliar.
explanation.walkthrough: Mathematicians use x, y and z for unknown quantities, so any of them can stand in for 'unknown'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sectary is a member or adherent of a sect, someone devoted to a particular religious group.

clue.text: Engineers are uncertain about stronghold

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to doubt something is to be uncertain about it

explanation.surface: Military engineers express misgivings about a fortification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a signal to put one piece round another, but it belongs with the phrase meaning doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a small fortification or a defended position, a place of last resort and safety.

clue.text: Study religious philosophy enthralling island inhabitant

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold someone captive, so one piece is held inside the rest

blocks.note: a den is a private study or room
Zen is a school of Buddhism
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Someone living on an island is captivated by studying Eastern religion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is a noun here, a small private room, not the verb it appears to be.
explanation.definitionFit: A denizen is a resident or regular occupant of a particular place, so it means an inhabitant.

clue.text: Detest river transport that's decrepit

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
a crate is slang for a rickety old car or aircraft

explanation.surface: Someone loathes a ramshackle old boat or ferry on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is a river in Devon, in south-west England. An old banger or plane is informally called a crate.
explanation.definitionFit: To execrate is to loathe or curse something, expressing utter abhorrence, so it means to detest.

clue.text: Flagrant prisoner cycling, on phone

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves a letter from one end of the word to the other

blocks.note: an old lag is a habitual convict
to phone someone is to ring them

explanation.surface: A brazen convict rides a bike while chatting on a mobile.
explanation.walkthrough: Moving the G of LAG from the back to the front gives GLA. 'Lag' is British slang for a prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A glaring error is a conspicuously obvious one, just as a flagrant breach is blatant.

clue.text: Ruled roof space, with centre hollowed out, to be turned into SA meeting place

indicators.note: hollowing out the centre scoops away the middle letter
something turned round faces the other way, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: to lead is to rule
an attic is a loft, here losing the middle T

explanation.surface: Instructions for converting an emptied attic into a venue for a South African gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: SA looks like South Africa but stands for the Salvation Army, whose local halls are called citadels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Salvation Army calls its corps buildings citadels, in keeping with its military-style ranks and terminology.

clue.text: Old measures in valleys

blocks.note: first meaning: an old dry measure for grain, four bushels
second meaning: short steep valleys in southern English chalk hills

explanation.surface: Historic distances being surveyed in the dales.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses take the same spelling, though the valley is also spelt combe or coomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A coomb was a former English unit of grain capacity, and also a hollow or deep valley on a hillside.

clue.text: One spouting off, chap on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word counts by its sound

blocks.note: geezer is British slang for a man or bloke

explanation.surface: A radio presenter keeps ranting on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spouting off' sounds like mouthing off, but a geyser literally spouts. Geezer is London slang for a man. In British English the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a hot spring that periodically erupts, shooting jets of boiling water skyward.

clue.text: What unscrupulous sellers do, extreme characters arrested by Hanks character

indicators.note: someone arrested is held in custody, so this piece is held inside

blocks.note: A and Z are the first and last letters of the alphabet
Tom Hanks played Forrest Gump

explanation.surface: Dodgy traders get nabbed by a role played by a Hollywood actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Gazumping is a British property practice: a seller accepts an offer and then takes a higher one before contracts are signed.
explanation.definitionFit: To gazump is to raise the price or accept a later bid after agreeing a sale, which is sharp dealing.

clue.text: Around old quarters, reshaped Zulu stone

indicators.note: things strewn around are scattered in no fixed order
something reshaped keeps its material but takes on a new form

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written
Zulu is Z in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Zulu craftsman reshapes stone in the old part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: Zulu is the radio code word for Z, so only that one letter joins the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose quartz is a pink variety of the mineral quartz, prized as a semi-precious gemstone.

clue.text: Rod stripped her naked

indicators.note: a stripped word loses its outer covering, so only the inside letters remain

blocks.note: a bar is a rod of metal
the central letter of her

explanation.surface: A man named Rod undressed a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name, but it is a metal bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare means without clothing or covering, exactly as naked does.

clue.text: Escape rubbish berth

blocks.note: first meaning: doing a runner
second meaning: nonsense, short for bunkum
third meaning: a narrow shelf bed on a ship or train

explanation.surface: Fleeing a squalid sleeping place on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in three words. 'Do a bunk' is British slang for running off.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a sleeping shelf, nonsense talk, and in British slang a quick getaway.

clue.text: Worthless vowel shift in noun governed by verb

indicators.note: shifting a vowel means swapping one vowel for a different one

blocks.note: in grammar the object is the noun a verb acts on

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson dismisses a sound change in a noun as pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening O is swapped for an A.
explanation.definitionFit: Abject describes something wretched and contemptible, of the lowest kind, so worthless fits.

clue.text: Name bird in memorandum

indicators.note: something in another sits within it, so one piece lies inside

blocks.note: mina is a variant spelling of myna, the Asian starling
a note is a short memorandum

explanation.surface: A memo identifies a particular bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The myna is often spelt mina or mynah in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: To nominate is to put forward or appoint someone by name, so the verb means to name.
